content.title: Earthquake: first five minutes
content.summary: Shaking starts while you are indoors. Practice protecting yourself, checking yourself and the people nearby before moving, and responding to an aftershock.
content.objective: Practice the first protective actions during and immediately after earthquake shaking.

sources.label: Earthquake Country Alliance (Great ShakeOut) — Drop, Cover, and Hold On

protected_during_shaking.text: You protected your head and neck and held on until the shaking stopped.

checked_immediate_hazards.text: You checked yourself and the people nearby, then lit your way and put on shoes before moving.

prepared_for_aftershock.text: You treated the aftershock like new shaking and protected yourself again.

needs_earthquake_drill.text: Practice your household's Drop, Cover, and Hold On positions together.

nodes.title: The room starts shaking
nodes.body: You are indoors when strong shaking begins. A sturdy table is a few steps away.

choices.label: Run outside before the shaking gets stronger
choices.consequence: The route outside passes windows and objects that are moving.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says: if you are inside, stay and do not run outside. Ready Kids says to stay away from windows, glass, and furniture that could fall.

choices.label: Drop, cover, and hold on—or lock wheels and cover if seated
choices.consequence: You protect your head and neck and hold on until the shaking stops.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to drop onto your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops. If a sturdy table is nearby, crawl under it. If you use a wheelchair or walker, lock your wheels if you can, get as low as possible, and cover your head and neck.

choices.label: Stand in the nearest doorway
choices.consequence: You stand in an open frame while objects in the room keep moving.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to avoid doorways. Take cover under a sturdy table, or next to an interior wall away from windows. The Earthquake Country Alliance says doorways in modern homes are no stronger than any other part of the house.

media.alt: An intact kitchen where a pendant lamp hangs at a strong angle, cups and a saucer have shifted apart on the counter, and a wall picture is tilted as strong shaking begins.

explanationMedia.alt: An adult and child shelter under a sturdy kitchen table, covering their heads and holding its legs; nearby, away from windows, a wheelchair user with locked wheels bends low and covers head and neck.

nodes.title: The shaking keeps going
nodes.body: The floor is still moving, and it is hard to stay on your feet. Books are sliding off the shelf by the window. A sturdy table is nearby.
nodes.prompt: What do you do while it is still shaking?

choices.label: Head for the front door
choices.consequence: You get partway across the room, past the window, while books keep falling.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says: if you are inside, stay and do not run outside. Drop where you are and cover your head and neck. Ready Kids says to stay away from windows and furniture that could fall.

choices.label: Stay standing and brace against the wall
choices.consequence: You sway with the floor while things keep falling nearby.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to protect yourself right away: drop onto your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and if a sturdy table is nearby, crawl under it and hold on.

choices.label: Get low where you are, or lock wheels if seated, and cover your head and neck
choices.consequence: You get low, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to drop where you are onto your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops. If you use a wheelchair or walker, lock your wheels if you can, get as low as possible, and cover your head and neck.

nodes.title: The shaking stops
nodes.body: The power is out. A few objects fell, and there is broken glass in the hall. You do not smell gas or see damage from where you are.
nodes.prompt: What do you do before moving around?

choices.label: Light a candle so you can inspect the room
choices.consequence: The candle adds an open flame before you have fully checked the area.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov lists leaking gas lines among the hazards after an earthquake. A flashlight gives light without an open flame.

choices.label: Check yourself and others, put on sturdy shoes, and use a flashlight
choices.consequence: You account for the people nearby and can see the floor before moving carefully.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to check yourself to see if you are hurt and help others if you have training. Ready Kids says to wear shoes to protect your skin from broken objects.

choices.label: Walk through the dark hall right away
choices.consequence: Broken glass and fallen objects make the dark route harder to judge.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov warns of serious hazards after an earthquake. Check yourself first, and put on shoes before walking near broken glass.

nodes.scene: 6:16 PM · Inside, right after the shaking

messages.text: Shaking here too. We're okay. Text when you can.

nodes.title: The room shakes again
nodes.body: As you are still moving around, an aftershock begins. A sturdy table is nearby.

choices.label: Keep inspecting because the first shaking is over
choices.consequence: Objects begin moving again while you keep inspecting.
choices.feedback: Ready Kids says aftershocks can come hours, days, or even months later. Protect yourself again whenever shaking starts.

choices.label: Head outside while the aftershock continues
choices.consequence: You cross the room past the window while objects shift again, and reach the front yard beside the house as it stops.
choices.feedback: Protect yourself where you are. Ready.gov says if you are inside, stay and do not run outside, and be ready to Drop, Cover and Hold On if you feel an aftershock.

choices.label: Drop, cover, and hold on again—or lock wheels and cover if seated
choices.consequence: You return to a protected position until the aftershock stops.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to expect aftershocks and be ready to Drop, Cover and Hold On if you feel one.

outcomes.title: You walked through the first five minutes
outcomes.body: You walked through the first minutes of an earthquake: the shaking, the moments after it stopped, and an aftershock. Ready.gov says to protect yourself right away: if you are inside, stay and do not run outside, and if you are outside, stay there. Before the aftershock, you saw no damage from where you were. Ready Kids says aftershocks could cause more damage to structures weakened by the first earthquake. If a building is damaged, Ready.gov says to go outside, quickly move away from it, and do not go back in. If you'd like, talk it over together: in each room you use most, where would each person take cover, under a sturdy table or next to an interior wall away from windows? Include anyone who uses a wheelchair, walker or cane.

outcomes.title: You walked through the first five minutes
outcomes.body: You walked through the first minutes of an earthquake: the shaking, the moments after it stopped, and an aftershock. Ready.gov says to protect yourself right away: if you are inside, stay and do not run outside, and if you are outside, stay there. You ended up outside, beside the house. The Earthquake Country Alliance says the area near a building's outside walls is the most dangerous place to be. If more shaking starts while you are outside, Ready.gov says to move to an open area away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines, and drop and cover until it stops. Ready.gov also says do not enter damaged buildings. If you'd like, talk it over together: if shaking starts while someone is already outside near home, where is an open area to stay in?
